stem: Each colour of the Olympic rings belongs to a particular continent, such as yellow for Asia.
explanation: No colour stands for any one continent. Pierre de Coubertin chose blue, yellow, black, green and red on white because every national flag of his day used at least one of them.

claims.text: The International Olympic Committee does not assign any ring colour to a particular continent.
The Olympic rings are blue, yellow, black, green and red on a white background, and were designed by Pierre de Coubertin.
Coubertin wrote, around 1913, that the six colours including the white background together reproduced the colours of every nation's flag at the time.

writerNotes: Subtopic: Olympic history and symbols. True/false myth, so the answer is false. lint: clean. claims: three; c1 high as the key of a counterintuitive item, c3 for its number. datasets: none applies; c1 and c3 need web evidence (the IOC's page on the Olympic rings, or Britannica). rivalTest: argued for 'true': the Olympic Charter says the five rings together represent the union of the five continents, which is why the colour-per-continent belief spreads. The statement is about each colour belonging to a continent, which the IOC does not say; the stem names a colour and a continent so it cannot be read as 'the rings as a whole stand for the continents'. volatility: evergreen. regional: the rings are recognized worldwide. style: Oxford spelling, explanation of 32 words. myths: screened; no entry on the Olympic rings in myths.json, so the editor may want to add one. mystery and encore: not applicable. doubts: the explanation's 'every national flag of his day' paraphrases Coubertin's 1913 claim; it is his claim, and the explanation presents it as his reason, not as a checked fact about every flag. Writer search (1 of the batch's 6): query 'IOC Olympic rings colours not linked to specific continent Coubertin flags of all nations'. The summary attributed to the IOC's FAQ (olympics.com/ioc/faq, Tier A) the statement that in 1913 the five colours with the white background represented the colours of the flags of all nations at that time, and to Olympics.com and Britannica that the colours do not represent any continent. It supports c1 and c3; no conflict reported.
